options.b: The flag is ignored and results arrive after the window has closed
options.c: It is refused with a validation error, since results come back as one file
options.d: The batch is accepted but billed at the full price of the live API

explanation.c: The page lists it (module 63, page 1): "Three parameters are refused with a validation error: `stream: true` (the results come back as one file, not a stream)".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the results come back as one file: "the results come back as one file, not a stream"
explanation.b: Ruled out because a batch finishes within a window: "A batch finishes within 24 hours (usually much sooner)"
explanation.d: Ruled out because the discount applies to work that can wait: "The half price is a reason to move work that can wait."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S2. A team proposes to log every tool result into the notes file during an exploration. Why is that wrong?

options.a: A file cannot be read back into a session once it has been written
options.b: Notes files are loaded into every session like an instructions file is
options.c: Working memory should hold findings, not a transcript, which is what filled the window
options.d: Tool results contain nothing that is worth keeping for later questions

explanation.c: The page states it (module 67, page 1): "it is not a transcript, which is the thing that filled the window in the first place".
explanation.a: Ruled out because later questions begin by reading it: "Later questions begin by reading the scratchpad"
explanation.b: Ruled out because the instructions file is another thing: "It is not a replacement for the project's instructions file, which holds what is true of the project for every session"
explanation.d: Ruled out because reading is what fills the window: "Exploration is the most context-hungry thing an agent does."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. On Wednesday an engineer wants to carry on Monday's exploration of the payments module as a single line of work. Which control fits?

options.a: Resume that session by its id, which adds to the original and keeps one thread
options.b: Fork the session, since a fork keeps the whole history and carries on the work
options.c: Continue the most recent session, which is the one from Monday
options.d: Start fresh with a prompt that asks the model to recall Monday from memory

explanation.a: The page separates the two (module 51, page 1): "Resume to continue one thread; fork to branch it."
explanation.b: Ruled out because a fork starts a second line: "a fork creates a new session with its own id, so the line of work now exists twice"
explanation.c: Ruled out because continue takes the newest: "Picks up the most recent session in the current directory and adds to it"
explanation.d: Ruled out because the history is what holds the earlier analysis: "A session is the conversation history the SDK accumulates while your agent works."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. Two forks of one session each try a refactor in the same working directory. What happens?

options.a: Each gets a private copy of the whole directory, so that the two attempts are isolated
options.b: Both edit the shared files, since branching copies the conversation and not the disk
options.c: The second is rejected at once, since a directory admits just one branch at a time
options.d: Their edits are merged automatically by the tool when the sessions end

explanation.b: The guide states the limit (module 51, page 1): "Forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem."
explanation.a: Ruled out because the changes are real and shared: "If a forked agent edits files, those changes are real and visible to any session working in the same directory."
explanation.c: Ruled out because nothing refuses the second: "Two forks that each try a refactor in the same working tree write over each other."
explanation.d: Ruled out because no merge happens: "Forking the session without isolating the files leaves both attempts editing the same checkout"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A service runs an exploration on one machine, and an engineer wants to continue it on a CI worker. What limits this?

options.a: Sessions can be resumed only by the account that created them, whatever host is used
options.b: A saved session expires after one hour of idleness and cannot be reopened
options.c: Only the Agent SDK can resume sessions, never the command line
options.d: Saved conversations stay on the host that wrote them, so copy them or use a digest

explanation.d: The page states it (module 51, page 1): "Session files are local to the machine that created them."
explanation.a: Ruled out because the limit is the machine and not the account: "You can resume from another directory on the same machine"
explanation.b: Ruled out because idleness only changes the cost: a session "has been inactive for more than about an hour and is over 100,000 tokens"
explanation.c: Ruled out because the command line can resume SDK sessions: "You can still resume one by passing its session ID to `claude --resume <session-id>`."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A process died while a tool call was running, and the session is resumed. What does the model see?

options.a: The operation flagged as interrupted before its outcome was stored, with a prompt to verify it
options.b: The call is finished again silently when the session resumes, without any notice
options.c: The call is shown as succeeded, since the process had already started it
options.d: The history is cut at the last completed message and the session carries on as normal

explanation.a: The page states it (module 51, page 2): the model "is told to check whether it took effect before running it again".
explanation.b: Ruled out because nothing runs again: "doesn't finish or run again when you resume"
explanation.c: Ruled out because a session does not mark old results: "Nothing in the session marks the old tool results as old."
explanation.d: Ruled out because a session holds the conversation and not the world: "Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A team denies Write(secrets/**) to keep the agent from changing a folder. Why does that protect nothing?

options.a: Deny rules apply only to shell commands and are not applied to any of the file tools
options.b: Folders that hold credentials are exempt from deny rules for reading and for writing
options.c: Deny rules are advisory, and the model may decide to ignore them when it sees fit
options.d: Path checks for modifications use the edit spelling, so a rule spelled the other way is never used

explanation.d: The page states it (module 56, page 2): "a `Write(path)` rule is never matched by the file permission checks".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the edit rules do cover file tools: "rules govern all built-in tools that write files"
explanation.b: Ruled out because a read deny is the strongest rule for such a folder: "A `Read` deny is the one rule that stops reading, searching and writing."
explanation.c: Ruled out because a deny is enforced by the harness, and what is not matched is the spelling: "Bash rules are matched as written."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A team scans code that an agent wrote for dangerous calls and runs it unattended whenever the scan is clean. What is wrong with relying on this alone?

options.a: Code written by a model cannot be read by any automatic check
options.b: A clean result proves nothing about what the code declares, so the proposal is ignored
options.c: Running it on every proposal costs too much, so it must be sampled
options.d: Detection covers only what its authors anticipated, so a disguised version slips past it

explanation.d: The page states it (module 77, page 1): "A scan finds what its authors thought of: a call spelled differently, built from strings or imported by name slips past it."
explanation.a: Ruled out because the gate does read generated code: "The gate in this module does read the code"
explanation.b: Ruled out because the scan does compare with the declaration: "it compares what the code does with what the proposal declares"
explanation.c: Ruled out because the scan is cheap: "and it costs nothing"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A tool design whose name breaks the required form also declares an effect that needs a person's sign-off. What should happen first?

options.a: It goes straight to the person, who can fix the name while approving
options.b: It returns for revision, so approval is asked only of a proposal worth reading
options.c: It is refused, since any format error is treated as a forbidden call
options.d: It is approved outright, since a name has no effect on safety

explanation.b: The page states it (module 77, page 2): "A revision comes before a gate, because a person should be asked to approve a proposal that is worth reading".
explanation.a: Ruled out because revision comes first: "A revision comes before a gate"
explanation.c: Ruled out because a format error only sends it back: "Four things only send it back: a name that is not in the fixed form"
explanation.d: Ruled out because only a clean proposal passes outright: "Only a proposal with none of these is approved outright."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A documentation tool's description is long, with its key rule in the last paragraph. What does Claude Code do with the text?

options.a: It reads all of it, since only the first sentence is shown to the user in the list, as a rule of the product
options.b: It summarises the description with a model call when the text is very long indeed
options.c: It truncates at 2,048 characters, so critical details should sit near the beginning
options.d: It rejects the server at launch with an error message naming the limit in force

explanation.c: The page states the limit (module 55, page 2): "Claude Code truncates each tool description and each server's instructions at 2,048 characters by default".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the cut is a fact: "Descriptions and server instructions are truncated at 2,048 characters by default."
explanation.b: Ruled out because the advice follows from it: "Keep them concise, and put critical details near the start."
explanation.d: Ruled out because the page names the effect: "The exam rejects the length: Claude Code truncates at 2,048 characters, so what you put last may be cut."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A skill from an installed plugin has the same folder name as a project skill. How can both be used?

options.a: The extension's is prefixed with its package label, so two separate commands exist
options.b: The project's overrides the plugin's, since committed files win over anything installed
options.c: The plugin's overrides the project's, since plugins are newer than the repository
options.d: Neither runs until one of them is renamed to remove the clash

explanation.a: The page lists the location (module 58, page 1): "with the name prefixed by the plugin's name".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the order of precedence is for skills that share a name: "Of skills that share a name"
explanation.c: Ruled out because a plugin skill is available where it is enabled: "Where the plugin is enabled"
explanation.d: Ruled out because a name clash has a winner: "`/deploy` runs the personal one"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A user-level file and a repository-level file give conflicting style advice. Which appears later in context?

options.a: The user-level one, since personal preferences are applied last in the order
options.b: Neither, since conflicting advice is dropped before anything is loaded
options.c: The more specific one, since loading runs from the broadest scope to the most specific
options.d: Whichever was edited most recently, since the loader sorts by time

explanation.c: The page states it (module 57, page 1): "from broadest scope to most specific, so a project instruction appears in context after a user instruction".
explanation.a: Ruled out because memory is advice and not an override: "Memory is advice with good delivery."
explanation.b: Ruled out because all discovered files are used: "All discovered files are concatenated into context"
explanation.d: Ruled out because order is by scope and not by time: "at the start of every session"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A skill lists disallowed-tools: Bash(rm *). What does that do while the skill is active?

options.a: It denies matching commands and keeps the shell available, since only a bare name removes it
options.b: It removes the shell from the available pool for the whole turn of the skill
options.c: It has no effect, since specifiers are ignored in the headers of skills
options.d: It blocks every command until the user sends the next message to the session

explanation.a: The page states it (module 58, page 2): "A bare tool name like `Bash` removes the tool from Claude's context entirely".
explanation.b: Ruled out because only a bare name removes a tool: "only a bare name removes a tool"
explanation.c: Ruled out because a scoped entry has an effect: "a scoped entry such as `Edit(src/**)` is a narrower rule that leaves the tool in place"
explanation.d: Ruled out because patterns are exact: "The patterns in `allowed-tools` are as exact as the rules in module 38"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A developer wants the built-in exploring subagent to dig deeply into a tangled module. What can the caller request?

options.a: A level of thoroughness, from quick through medium to very thorough
options.b: A write permission, from none to full access to the whole tree of the project
options.c: A larger window, from standard to extended for the long search
options.d: A count of files to read, from ten up to a thousand files

explanation.a: The page states it (module 67, page 1): "The caller can ask for a thoroughness (quick, medium or very thorough)."
explanation.b: Ruled out because it is read-only: "with Write and Edit denied"
explanation.c: Ruled out because the cost of reading is the window: "Exploration is the most context-hungry thing an agent does."
explanation.d: Ruled out because the question has to be specific: "The question must be specific"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A large exploration moves from mapping modules to tracing flows. How should the findings of the first phase reach the second?

options.a: A digest from the notes goes into the opening prompts of the later workers
options.b: Pass the full transcript of the first phase to each second-phase worker so that nothing is lost
options.c: Let the second phase rediscover them, since fresh eyes avoid bias
options.d: Keep the first phase's workers running and reuse their windows

explanation.a: The page states it (module 67, page 1): "The coordinator summarises the first phase's findings (from the scratchpad) and puts that summary into the initial prompts of the second phase's subagents."
explanation.b: Ruled out because the transcript is what filled the window: "It does not get the old transcript, which is what filled the first window."
explanation.c: Ruled out because one phase starts from the next: "The findings of one phase are the starting point of the next."
explanation.d: Ruled out because a worker does not inherit anything: "the brief must carry what the subagent needs, because it does not inherit the conversation"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A manager tells a helper to explore the whole repository and gets back a long account. What was wrong with the delegation?

options.a: The helper should have been given write access so that it could keep notes
options.b: The helper's window was too small for such a long search of the tree
options.c: The brief was too broad, so the reply gave its author nothing new
options.d: The summary should have been requested in a table instead of prose

explanation.c: The page states it (module 67, page 1): "The question must be specific".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the explorer is read-only by design: "with Write and Edit denied"
explanation.b: Ruled out because a helper reads in a separate window of its own: "Subagents run in separate context windows"
explanation.d: Ruled out because the brief has to carry what the helper needs: "the brief must carry what the subagent needs, because it does not inherit the conversation"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S4. A coordinator runs five sources in order, and the second fails with a timeout. The run stops there. What does that waste?

options.a: Everything scheduled after the broken one, whose work was never done
options.b: Only the failed source's partial results, which were small anyway and a little context
options.c: Nothing, since later sources depend on the second one
options.d: The retry budget, which is reset by stopping

explanation.a: The page states it (module 66, page 1): "aborting on the first failure throws away every source after the failing one".
explanation.b: Ruled out because partial results are work already done: "Discarding them wastes work the subagent did"
explanation.c: Ruled out because a failed topic does not end the plan: "There is no entry that ends the run."
explanation.d: Ruled out because a transient failure is the worker's to retry: "A transient failure, a timeout or a brief outage, is the subagent's to retry"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A normalising hook runs twice on the same result, for instance when a result is replayed. Which property should it have?

options.a: Determinism across tools: the same date shape is applied to each field that it sees
options.b: Statelessness: it must not read the tool input of the call that it handles
options.c: Idempotence: an already readable value is left alone and the answer stays empty
options.d: Atomicity: it must write the fields together or not write any of them

explanation.c: The page lists the rule (module 49, page 2): "A value that is already readable is not touched".
explanation.a: Ruled out because changing everything is the opposite of the rule: "Change only what you understand."
explanation.b: Ruled out because a hook reads the input and the id that ties events together: "the tool use id that ties a pre and a post event together"
explanation.d: Ruled out because unknown fields pass: "Fields that are not in the table pass through as they were."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A team registers a hook with the matcher Write|Edit. How is that value read?

options.a: As a regular expression that also matches names containing either word in the middle
options.b: As a list of two exact tool names, because it holds only letters and a pipe
options.c: As a path filter for the locations that those tools write to disk
options.d: As a request to match both names only when they occur in the same turn

explanation.b: The page gives the syntax (module 49, page 1): "A value with only letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, spaces, commas and pipes is read as an exact name or a list of exact names".
explanation.a: Ruled out because only other values are expressions: "anything else is read as a regular expression"
explanation.c: Ruled out because matchers see names and nothing else: "Matchers only match tool names, not file paths or other arguments."
explanation.d: Ruled out because no matcher means every event: "Hooks without a matcher run for every event of that type"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A fan-out runs one extraction pass per document, then a cross-check pass over their summaries. One of twelve passes fails. What should the run do?

options.a: Abort the whole run, since one failure makes the rest unreliable
options.b: Log it with its message, carry on with the rest, and exclude it from the last step
options.c: Retry that one forever until it succeeds, then continue
options.d: Give the last step an empty summary for it, so that the count stays complete in the report

explanation.b: The page states it (module 50, page 2): "The practice records it (path and message) and goes on with the others, and it leaves the failed file out of the cross pass."
explanation.a: Ruled out because a failure belongs to its item: "a failure in one is a fact about that file"
explanation.c: Ruled out because a loop with no bound never ends: "A loop with no bound turns a service outage into a run that never ends."
explanation.d: Ruled out because only reviewed items reach the last pass: "The cross pass sees only the files that were reviewed"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. Logs of an extraction agent show many redundant tool calls and few errors. What does the article suggest?

options.a: Rewrite the descriptions with clearer examples
options.b: Remove half of the tools so that fewer calls are possible
options.c: Raise the output ceiling so that each call returns more
options.d: Rightsize the pagination or token limit parameters

explanation.d: The page quotes the article (module 52, page 2): "Lots of redundant tool calls might suggest some rightsizing of pagination or token limit parameters is warranted".
explanation.a: Ruled out because errors, not repeats, point at descriptions: "lots of tool errors for invalid parameters might suggest tools could use clearer descriptions or better examples"
explanation.b: Ruled out because the article warns about overlap and not about a count: "Too many tools or overlapping tools can also distract agents from pursuing efficient strategies."
explanation.c: Ruled out because a response should be lean: "Design tool responses to return only high-signal information."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. An extraction tool's write to a store times out after the request left, and the store honours idempotency keys. Which retry is safe?

options.a: Resend with a new token each time, so that every attempt is tracked
options.b: Never resend, because any timeout means that the write failed
options.c: Resend with the identical token on every attempt, so the action is performed once
options.d: Resend without a token, since the store deduplicates by content

explanation.c: The page lists the safe cases (module 53, page 2): "A call that carries an idempotency key that the service honours."
explanation.a: Ruled out because the same key is the point: "The tool sends the same key on every attempt, and the service performs the action once"
explanation.b: Ruled out because a timeout is news-free: "A timeout after sending is not a failure of the effect; it is the absence of news."
explanation.d: Ruled out because without a key the call is unsafe: "Everything else is unsafe"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. An extraction stores for each field the quote it came from. What does a passing check prove?

options.a: That the value is correct, since the quote came from the source
options.b: That the model is confident, since it supplied a quote
options.c: That the schema is valid, since provenance is a required object
options.d: That the value is grounded in the text, not that it is correct

explanation.d: The page limits the check (module 62, page 1): "Provenance does not prove a value is correct, only that it is grounded".
explanation.a: Ruled out because other checks cover correctness: "the sum check and the review of conflicts cover the rest"
explanation.b: Ruled out because the test is plain code: "it does not ask the model whether it is right"
explanation.c: Ruled out because provenance is part of the shape: "a required `provenance` object that maps each field to a quote"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A schema gives a missing vendor name the default unknown. Why does that hurt downstream?

options.a: It breaks the parser, since a string is not allowed for that field in the schema
options.b: It lowers accuracy in the report, since defaults count as errors
options.c: It forces the model to guess the vendor on every record
options.d: Code cannot tell it from a real value, so a placeholder passes as genuine

explanation.d: The page gives the reason (module 62, page 1): "downstream code cannot tell it from a real value".
explanation.a: Ruled out because the parse is fine: "The JSON never fails to parse."
explanation.b: Ruled out because a clean record passes: "A pipeline that stops at schema validation reports a high success rate and passes wrong records on."
explanation.c: Ruled out because nullability is the remedy: "a field that may be missing from the source is optional or nullable"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A team plans a weekly extraction over thousands of stored documents and wants the lowest cost. Which interface fits, and what must each entry carry?

options.a: Batch processing, with a unique custom_id per request so that results match their inputs
options.b: The synchronous interface with streaming, since results arrive sooner that way
options.c: Batch processing with stream set to true, so that results arrive one by one
options.d: The synchronous interface in parallel threads, since discounts need a contract

explanation.a: The page names the shape (module 63, page 1): "A batch entry is `{custom_id, params}`, where `params` are the parameters of a Messages request."
explanation.b: Ruled out because the discount is for work that can wait: "The half price is a reason to move work that can wait."
explanation.c: Ruled out because streaming is refused: "the results come back as one file, not a stream"
explanation.d: Ruled out because standard documents belong in the queue: "Standard documents go to the batch queue"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A pipeline's overall accuracy clears its target, and the team proposes dropping manual review for everything. What does the page say decides this?

options.a: The overall average, since a figure above target covers every kind
options.b: Evidence for each kind of input, never the average
options.c: The workload that reviewers face in a normal week
options.d: The model's own confidence on each record it returns

explanation.b: The page states it (module 75, page 1): "decided by evidence for each kind, never by the average."
explanation.a: Ruled out because an average can hide a hopeless kind: "The dashboard says 99 percent and the reviewers say handwriting is hopeless"
explanation.c: Ruled out because a workload is not evidence: "decided by evidence for each kind"
explanation.d: Ruled out because confidence is not the test: "The status is derived from the checks, and the model's own opinion plays no part."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A record has the currency other and no currency_detail. How does the pipeline classify it?

options.a: As a semantic error, since the value is plausible but unchecked
options.b: As a syntax error, because the pair is the contract
options.c: As valid, since other is a member of the enum
options.d: As an absent value that goes straight to review untried

explanation.b: The page states it (module 62, page 1): "A record with `other` and no detail is a syntax error, because the pair is the contract."
explanation.a: Ruled out because semantic errors are about meaning: "a vendor in the currency field"
explanation.c: Ruled out because other comes with its detail: "`other` plus a detail field for a value the enum did not foresee"
explanation.d: Ruled out because absence is another case: "A required value that the model reports as absent is not retried: the document goes to review"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A batch's results file lists entries in a different order from the requests. How should the pipeline pair each result with its request?

options.a: By position, since results mirror the sequence in which the entries were sent to the batch service
options.b: By matching the text of each answer against the text of each prompt sent
options.c: By the unique label that each submission carries, because sequence is not promised
options.d: By timestamps, since the earliest request normally finishes first

explanation.c: The page states it (module 63, page 1): "it is the only link between a request and its result".
explanation.a: Ruled out because results come in any order: "can be returned in any order"
explanation.b: Ruled out because the label is a short identifier: "The `custom_id` is 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, hyphens and underscores"
explanation.d: Ruled out because each entry has its own result: "A finished batch has a result per entry: succeeded, errored, canceled or expired."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. One pass reports the same defect twice, and another pass reports it once. How many independent confirmations are there?

options.a: Two, since a reviewer that repeats itself still counts as one voice
options.b: Three, since each report of the defect is a confirmation
options.c: One, since the second reviewer only repeats the first one
options.d: Zero, since independent confirmation needs at least three reviewers

explanation.a: The page states it (module 63, page 2): "A pass that reports it twice counts once, since repetition inside a pass is not independent evidence."
explanation.b: Ruled out because identity is by file, line and issue: "The same finding, identified by file, line and issue, reported by two passes is one finding."
explanation.c: Ruled out because independence is about the reviewer: "A reviewer is independent if it could not have copied the author's rationale."
explanation.d: Ruled out because passes produce lists that are combined by rules: "Several independent passes produce several lists."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. On a labelled set, no confidence cut-off reaches the 95% target. What follows?

options.a: Use the cut-off with the highest precision and automate everything above it
options.b: Lower the target until some cut-off qualifies for automation
options.c: Ask the model to restate its confidence on a hundred-point scale
options.d: Every item needs review until the pipeline improves, since no honest boundary exists

explanation.d: The page states it (module 68, page 1): "If no threshold reaches the target, there is no honest cut-off: every item needs review until the pipeline improves."
explanation.a: Ruled out because the rule picks the lowest qualifying threshold: "The lowest qualifying threshold automates the most work while meeting the target."
explanation.b: Ruled out because a threshold has to reach the target: "Pick the lowest threshold whose precision reaches the target."
explanation.c: Ruled out because a restated number is still a score: "The number is only a score"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. A subagent cannot name a source for a statement that the schema demands one for. What should it do?

options.a: Invent a plausible citation so that the schema validates the finding
options.b: Cite the search engine as the source of each unsourced claim
options.c: Return it as a finding with an empty reference field and a warning
options.d: Report it apart as lacking an origin, or omit it, rather than return it as a finding

explanation.d: The page states it (module 69, page 1): "A subagent that cannot name a source for a statement does not return it as a finding: it reports it separately as unsourced, or leaves it out".
explanation.a: Ruled out because a required field pushes toward invention: "a required field pushes a model to invent a value when there is none"
explanation.b: Ruled out because a source travels with its claim: "A source survives as long as it travels with its claim in a field."
explanation.c: Ruled out because a finding without a source is refused on entry: "a finding without one is refused where it enters the pipeline"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S6. Six extraction workers may be lost to a restart. When should each write its state file?

options.a: As it learns, so that a crash half-way still leaves something
options.b: At the end only, when its findings are complete and checked
options.c: Once an hour on a timer, whatever it has learned in that time
options.d: Only when a person asks for a checkpoint of its work

explanation.a: The page states it (module 67, page 2): "It is written as the agent learns and not only at the end, so that a crash half-way leaves something."
explanation.b: Ruled out because a crash gives no warning: "A crash does not warn."
explanation.c: Ruled out because the file holds findings in a fixed form: "holding its findings in the scratchpad form of page 1: specific, once, grouped"
explanation.d: Ruled out because the path is fixed by the design: "Each agent exports its state to a known location"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A loop checks a turn limit before every model call. On one run the limit is ten, and the tenth reply ends its turn with a full answer. Which status should a correct loop report?

options.a: Max turns, because the number of calls reached the limit on that very reply of the run
options.b: Truncated, because the loop made its last permitted request and must therefore assume that the text was cut off
options.c: Unexpected, because a loop that has no call left cannot confirm how the reply ended
options.d: Done, because the tally was tested before that last request and nothing was cut

explanation.d: The page puts the check where it protects the last call (module 45, page 1): "a reply that ends the turn on the very last allowed call is still done".
explanation.a: Ruled out because a reply that ended its turn is finished, and the count is only a backstop: "Keep the count as a backstop, above the real need, with a status that is not `done`."
explanation.b: Ruled out because a reply that ended its turn is not cut off, since the page reads that stop reason as "Claude finished its response naturally."
explanation.c: Ruled out because a known value is handled by name: "in your own code, give every other value a status of its own."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A reply that describes a refund policy ends with the stop reason `max_tokens`, in the middle of a sentence. What should the loop do?

options.a: Treat the run as finished, since the model stopped producing tool calls
options.b: Leave with a status of its own, because the output was cut off and a higher ceiling is the code's call
options.c: Call the model again at once with identical messages, since a cut-off reply is a transient fault of the service
options.d: Ask the model to repeat the answer in fewer words, since the ceiling is the reply's fault

explanation.b: The page lists the value (module 45, page 1): "Leave with a status of its own: the reply is cut off, and raising the limit is a decision for your code".
explanation.a: Ruled out because a cut-off reply is not a finished one: "Leave with a status of its own: the reply is cut off, and raising the limit is a decision for your code"
explanation.c: Ruled out because the loop continues on one value only: "Run the calls and send the results; this is the only value that continues"
explanation.d: Ruled out because the loop does not guess at an unknown reason: "A value the loop has never seen must not be guessed at."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A pre-call hook denies refunds above 500. The hook returns a short sentence that the model reads before it decides what to tell the customer. Which reason should it return to the model?

options.a: Forbidden by company policy for this kind of request
options.b: Amounts over that limit go to a person, so hand this case over
options.c: Permission denied for the requested action by the rules
options.d: Blocked for now: please retry the same call again in a moment or two, after a short pause

explanation.b: The page prefers a reason that teaches (module 49, page 1): a reason "tells the model what to do next, which is the same design as the refusal sentence of module 48".
explanation.a: Ruled out because a bare refusal says nothing to do: "A reason is part of the interface."
explanation.c: Ruled out because a flat denial ends the attempt: "Writing to /etc is not allowed"
explanation.d: Ruled out because the reason "tells the model why, so it avoids retrying."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A hook converts epoch seconds to dates in order results. A tool returns a plain-text error. What should the hook do?

options.a: Parse it as JSON and fill the missing fields with defaults so that the shape is uniform for the next stage
options.b: Replace it with a tidy message so that every result looks the same
options.c: Raise an exception, so that the call is retried by the loop
options.d: Pass it through unchanged with an empty answer, since rewriting it would hide the failure

explanation.d: The page limits the normaliser (module 49, page 2): "since rewriting an error hides the failure".
explanation.a: Ruled out because it changes only what it understands: "Fields that are not in the table pass through as they were."
explanation.b: Ruled out because the page rejects it by name: "Normalise by rewriting every result, errors included."
explanation.c: Ruled out because a crash is not a repair: "A guard that crashes on unexpected input is therefore a guard that lets the call through."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A hook script blocks a refund by exiting with code 2 and also prints a JSON decision. What does the guide advise?

options.a: Always print the JSON as well, since the exit code alone is ignored
options.b: Choose a single style for that component, since mixing leaves the winner to the reference
options.c: Prefer the exit code and discard the JSON, because the code is read first
options.d: Print the JSON first and exit with 2 afterwards so that both are recorded

explanation.b: The page quotes the guide (module 49, page 2): "Use exit 2 to block with a stderr message, or exit 0 with JSON for structured control. Choose one approach per hook."
explanation.a: Ruled out because the winner is left open: "Mixing them leaves it to the reference to say which wins, and a guard should not depend on that."
explanation.c: Ruled out because the reason of a block goes to stderr: "Where the reason lands depends on the event"
explanation.d: Ruled out because with exit 0 the JSON decides: "No objection from the exit code; with JSON printed on standard output, the JSON decides"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. An agent's loop answers two tool calls that came in one reply. In what shape must the results go back?

options.a: Together in one user message, with those blocks placed before any added text
options.b: In separate user messages, one per call, in the order the calls were made by the model itself
options.c: In one assistant message, since the model asked for the work
options.d: In one user message, with explanatory text first and the blocks after it

explanation.a: The page gives the shape (module 45, page 2): "the tool_result blocks must come FIRST in the content array."
explanation.b: Ruled out because one message answers the whole turn: "A turn with three calls gets one user message with three results"
explanation.c: Ruled out because the answer is a user message: "Tool result blocks must immediately follow their corresponding tool use blocks in the message history"
explanation.d: Ruled out because blocks come first: "the tool_result blocks must come FIRST in the content array."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A loop receives a reply whose stop reason is stop_sequence. The setup lists two custom endings for a generation. What should it do?

options.a: Continue with the next request, since only an end of turn means that the work is finished
options.b: Raise the output ceiling and ask again with the same messages
options.c: Treat it as finished, and check which of the configured strings fired if that matters
options.d: Report an unexpected value that needs an alert and a person to look at it

explanation.c: The page gives the action (module 45, page 1): "Leave: done, and read which sequence fired".
explanation.a: Ruled out because only one value continues: "Run the calls and send the results; this is the only value that continues"
explanation.b: Ruled out because a cut-off is another value: "Leave with a status of its own: the reply is cut off, and raising the limit is a decision for your code"
explanation.d: Ruled out because this value is known: "A value the loop has never seen must not be guessed at."

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A lookup finds no orders for a customer. The customer exists, but no purchase was made in the period that was searched. Which reply is right?

options.a: An error result flagged as not found, so that the agent tries another route through the other service
options.b: An empty string, so that the agent decides what it means
options.c: A successful response saying that nothing matched the identifier and the date range
options.d: A transient error with retry set, in case the index is catching up

explanation.c: The page treats it as success (module 53, page 1): "A lookup that finds no orders for a customer has worked."
explanation.a: Ruled out because a failure and an empty answer are different: "from a valid empty result, which is a successful query that found no matches"
explanation.b: Ruled out because the two replies mean opposite things: "The two replies look alike in a log and mean opposite things"
explanation.d: Ruled out because a transient failure is a timeout or a limit: "A timeout, an unavailable service, a rate limit: the same call may work soon"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. The wrapper has no information yet about the state of the remote system. Which of these calls may be sent again after a timeout without first checking state?

options.a: An email send, because the outbox accepted it before the timeout occurred
options.b: A refund that carries an idempotency key which the service honours
options.c: A refund with no key, because the amount is validated
options.d: A ticket creation, because duplicates can be merged later

explanation.b: The page lists the safe cases (module 53, page 2): "A call that carries an idempotency key that the service honours."
explanation.a: Ruled out because a sent email cannot be recalled: "an email that left the outbox cannot be called back"
explanation.c: Ruled out because validation does not prevent a second payment: "a refund sent twice refunds twice"
explanation.d: Ruled out because a duplicate is real: "a ticket created twice is two tickets"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A refund call fails with a permission error, and the loop retries it three times. The error text says that the caller lacks the right to issue refunds. What went wrong?

options.a: Only a person with authority settles it, so repeating puts a human question to a machine
options.b: Three is too many, and a single retry after a short pause would have succeeded
options.c: The error should have been marked as a validation failure by the tool author
options.d: The loop should have retried with a different amount each time it failed

explanation.a: The page states it (module 53, page 1): "a loop that retries a permission failure three times has asked a person's question of a machine three times".
explanation.b: Ruled out because a transient fault is the kind that clears: "A timeout, an unavailable service, a rate limit: the same call may work soon"
explanation.c: Ruled out because the two failures are repaired differently: "but the agent repairs one and escalates the other"
explanation.d: Ruled out because a validation failure is about the input: "The input was wrong: a missing field, a value out of range, a bad format"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A support agent's tools come from a billing service and a shipping service, and both define a tool named lookup. How should the names be set?

options.a: Rename them lookup1 and lookup2, since numbers keep the labels short and unique across the whole catalogue
options.b: Begin each one with the system it belongs to, so that each family is easy to tell apart
options.c: Keep both as lookup and rely on the descriptions to separate them in each turn
options.d: Merge them into one lookup that tries both of the services in turn

explanation.b: The page quotes the documentation (module 52, page 1): "When your tools span multiple services or resources, prefix names with the service (for example, `github_list_prs`, `slack_send_message`)."
explanation.a: Ruled out because a name is the first thing the model reads: "A name is the first thing the model reads."
explanation.c: Ruled out because near-identical texts leave nothing to choose by: "Two tools whose texts say nearly the same thing leave the model nothing to choose by"
explanation.d: Ruled out because a merge is a larger change: "it is a larger change than a first step needs"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. An organisation wants data-handling reminders delivered to every machine and wants a particular shell command blocked. Which pairing is right?

options.a: A managed memory document for both, since individual settings cannot exclude it
options.b: Managed settings for both, since they carry text and rules alike
options.c: A managed memory document for the text and managed settings for the prohibition
options.d: A user-level memory document for both, pushed by a login script

explanation.c: The page separates them (module 57, page 1): "blocking a tool, a command or a path is done with managed settings".
explanation.a: Ruled out because memory is context and not enforcement: "Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration"
explanation.b: Ruled out because a managed memory file is for behaviour: "A managed CLAUDE.md is for behaviour"
explanation.d: Ruled out because a user-level file is personal: "You, in every project"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A support assistant's role is set in one sentence of the system prompt. What does the documentation say about such a sentence?

options.a: It carries no weight unless a page of rules follows it
options.b: It overrides each instruction that appears later in the conversation
options.c: A brief line is enough to make a difference to focus and tone
options.d: It applies to the first reply of a session and then lapses

explanation.c: The page quotes the documentation (module 76, page 1): "Setting a role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case. Even a single sentence makes a difference."
explanation.a: Ruled out because a persona needs little: "A persona needs a name, a manner and its limits, not a page of rules"
explanation.b: Ruled out because rules that must hold belong elsewhere: "the rules that must hold belong in the s"
explanation.d: Ruled out because a role focuses behaviour for the use case: "focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A support team wants a reviewer that shares none of the refund assistant's reasoning. What gives the product that building block?

options.a: A second turn in the same conversation with a stricter instruction
options.b: A larger thinking budget given to the same session
options.c: A separate helper that begins with a fresh window and hands back only a summary
options.d: A copy of the conversation passed to a new instance with the notes attached for its own reading

explanation.c: The page states it (module 63, page 1): "In Claude Code a subagent starts with a fresh context window that does not include the conversation history, the skills already invoked or the files the main agent has read, and returns only a summary."
explanation.a: Ruled out because a stricter instruction leaves the reasoning in place: "a stricter instruction in the same conversation, since the reasoning is still there"
explanation.b: Ruled out because more room is the same starting point: "a larger thinking budget, which gives the model more room to reason from the same starting point"
explanation.d: Ruled out because the reviewer gets the code and not the reasoning: "the code, and not the reasoning"

quizzes.stem: Scenario S1. A long input holds twenty order summaries and a question. Where should the question and the key facts go?

options.a: The question at the start, so that the model reads it before the summaries
options.b: The ask at the end, with a short digest of the essentials at the start
options.c: Both in the middle, where the attention of the model is strongest
options.d: The question repeated after every summary so that it is never forgotten

explanation.b: The page states it (module 64, page 1): "Put the long material first and the question last."
explanation.a: Ruled out because the middle is where findings go missing: "a long input's middle is where findings go missing"
explanation.c: Ruled out because detail goes under headers: "Organise the detail under explicit headers"
explanation.d: Ruled out because quoting before answering is another tool: "Asking the model to quote the relevant passages before answering is a fourth tool for long documents."
